367:     /// Attempt to do a fast confirmation of a word match that covers a subset
368:     /// (but hopefully a big subset) of most cases. Ok(Some(..)) is returned
369:     /// when a match is found. Ok(None) is returned when there is definitively
370:     /// no match. Err(()) is returned when this routine could not detect
371:     /// whether there was a match or not.
372:     pub(crate) fn fast_find(
373:         &self,
374:         word: &WordMatcher,
375:         haystack: &[u8],
376:         at: usize,
377:     ) -> Result<Option<Match>, ()> {
378:         // This is a bit hairy. The whole point here is to avoid running a
379:         // slower regex engine to extract capture groups. Remember, our word
380:         // regex looks like this:
381:         //
382:         //     (^|\W)(<original regex>)(\W|$)
383:         //
384:         // What we want are the match offsets of <original regex>. So in the
385:         // easy/common case, the original regex will be sandwiched between
386:         // two codepoints that are in the \W class. So our approach here is to
387:         // look for a match of the overall word regexp, strip the \W ends and
388:         // then check whether the original regex matches what's left. If so,
389:         // then we are guaranteed a correct match.
390:         //
391:         // This only works though if we know that the match is sandwiched
392:         // between two \W codepoints. This only occurs when neither ^ nor $
393:         // match. This in turn only occurs when the match is at either the
394:         // beginning or end of the haystack. In either of those cases, we
395:         // declare defeat and defer to the slower implementation.
396:         //
397:         // The reason why we cannot handle the ^/$ cases here is because we
398:         // can't assume anything about the original pattern. (Try commenting
399:         // out the checks for ^/$ below and run the tests to see examples.)
400:         let config = self.config();
401:         let unicode = config.unicode;
402:         let crlf = config.crlf;
403:         let line_terminator = config.line_terminator;
404: 
405:         let input = Input::new(haystack).span(at..haystack.len());
406:         let search_start = input.start();
407:         let search_end = input.end();
408:         let haystack = input.haystack();
409:         let input = Input::new(haystack).span(search_start..search_end);
410: 
411:         let mut cand = match word.regex().find(input) {
412:             None => return Ok(None),
413:             Some(m) => Match::new(m.start(), m.end()),
414:         };
415:         let at_haystack_edge = if crlf {
416:             cand.start() == 0 || cand.end() == haystack.len()
417:         } else if unicode {
418:             cand.start() == 0 || cand.end() == haystack.len()
419:         } else {
420:             cand.start() == 0 || cand.end() == haystack.len()
421:         };
422:         let at_terminator_edge = match line_terminator {
423:             Some(lt) => {
424:                 cand.end() == haystack.len()
425:                     && cand.end() > 0
426:                     && haystack[cand.end() - 1] == lt.as_byte()
427:             }
428:             None => false,
429:         };
430:         if at_haystack_edge || at_terminator_edge {
431:             return Err(());
432:         }
433:         let (_, slen) = bstr::decode_utf8(&haystack[cand]);
434:         let (_, elen) = bstr::decode_last_utf8(&haystack[cand]);
435:         let new_start = cand.start() + slen;
436:         let new_end = cand.end() - elen;
437:         // This occurs the original regex can match the empty string. In this
438:         // case, just bail instead of trying to get it right here since it's
439:         // likely a pathological case.
440:         if new_start > new_end {
441:             return Err(());
442:         }
443:         cand = cand.with_start(new_start).with_end(new_end);
444:         if word.original().is_match(&haystack[cand]) {
445:             Ok(Some(cand))
446:         } else {
447:             Err(())
448:         }
449:     }
450: }

452: /// This increments the index of every capture group in the given hir by 1. If
453: /// any increment results in an overflow, then an error is returned.
454: fn renumber_capture_indices(hir: Hir) -> Result<Hir, Error> {
455:     Ok(match hir.into_kind() {
456:         HirKind::Empty => Hir::empty(),
457:         HirKind::Literal(hir::Literal(lit)) => Hir::literal(lit),
458:         HirKind::Class(cls) => Hir::class(cls),
459:         HirKind::Look(x) => Hir::look(x),
460:         HirKind::Repetition(mut x) => {
461:             x.sub = Box::new(renumber_capture_indices(*x.sub)?);
462:             Hir::repetition(x)
463:         }
464:         HirKind::Capture(mut cap) => {
465:             cap.index = match cap.index.checked_add(1) {
466:                 Some(index) => index,
467:                 None => {
468:                     // This error message kind of sucks, but it's probably
469:                     // impossible for it to happen. The only way a capture
470:                     // index can overflow addition is if the regex is huge
471:                     // (or something else has gone horribly wrong).
472:                     let msg = "could not renumber capture index, too big";
473:                     return Err(Error::any(msg));
474:                 }
475:             };
476:             cap.sub = Box::new(renumber_capture_indices(*cap.sub)?);
477:             Hir::capture(cap)
478:         }
479:         HirKind::Concat(subs) => {
480:             let subs = subs
481:                 .into_iter()
482:                 .map(|sub| renumber_capture_indices(sub))
483:                 .collect::<Result<Vec<Hir>, Error>>()?;
484:             Hir::concat(subs)
485:         }
486:         HirKind::Alternation(subs) => {
487:             let subs = subs
488:                 .into_iter()
489:                 .map(|sub| renumber_capture_indices(sub))
490:                 .collect::<Result<Vec<Hir>, Error>>()?;
491:             Hir::alternation(subs)
492:         }
493:     })
494: }

499:     if lineterm.is_crlf() {
500:         literal.as_bytes().iter().copied().any(|b| b == b'\r' || b == b'\n')
501:     } else {
502:         literal.as_bytes().iter().copied().any(|b| b == lineterm.as_byte())
503:     }
504: }

15: /// Config represents the configuration of a regex matcher in this crate.

18: /// options.

21: /// configured HIR expression is an HIR expression that is aware of the
22: /// configuration which generated it, and provides transformation on that HIR
23: /// such that the configuration is preserved.

70:     /// Use this configuration to build an HIR from the given patterns. The HIR
71:     /// returned corresponds to a single regex that is an alternation of the
72:     /// patterns given.
73:     pub(crate) fn build_many<P: AsRef<str>>(
74:         &self,
75:         patterns: &[P],
76:     ) -> Result<ConfiguredHIR, Error> {
77:         ConfiguredHIR::new(self.clone(), patterns)
78:     }
79: 
80:     /// Accounting for the `smart_case` config knob, return true if and only if
81:     /// this pattern should be matched case insensitively.
82:     fn is_case_insensitive(&self, analysis: &AstAnalysis) -> bool {
83:         if self.case_insensitive {
84:             return true;
85:         }
86:         if !self.case_smart {
87:             return false;
88:         }
89:         analysis.any_literal() && !analysis.any_uppercase()
90:     }
91: 
92:     /// Returns whether the given patterns should be treated as "fixed strings"
93:     /// literals. This is different from just querying the `fixed_strings` knob
94:     /// in that if the knob is false, this will still return true in some cases
95:     /// if the patterns are themselves indistinguishable from literals.
96:     ///
97:     /// The main idea here is that if this returns true, then it is safe
98:     /// to build an `regex_syntax::hir::Hir` value directly from the given
99:     /// patterns as an alternation of `hir::Literal` values.
100:     fn is_fixed_strings<P: AsRef<str>>(&self, patterns: &[P]) -> bool {
101:         // When these are enabled, we really need to parse the patterns and
102:         // let them go through the standard HIR translation process in order
103:         // for case folding transforms to be applied.
104:         if self.case_insensitive || self.case_smart {
105:             return false;
106:         }
107:         // Even if whole_line or word is enabled, both of those things can
108:         // be implemented by wrapping the Hir generated by an alternation of
109:         // fixed string literals. So for here at least, we don't care about the
110:         // word or whole_line settings.
111:         if self.fixed_strings {
112:             // ... but if any literal contains a line terminator, then we've
113:             // got to bail out because this will ultimately result in an error.
114:             if let Some(lineterm) = self.line_terminator {
115:                 for p in patterns.iter() {
116:                     if has_line_terminator(lineterm, p.as_ref()) {
117:                         return false;
118:                     }
119:                 }
120:             }
121:             return true;
122:         }
123:         // In this case, the only way we can hand construct the Hir is if none
124:         // of the patterns contain meta characters. If they do, then we need to
125:         // send them through the standard parsing/translation process.
126:         for p in patterns.iter() {
127:             let p = p.as_ref();
128:             if p.chars().any(regex_syntax::is_meta_character) {
129:                 return false;
130:             }
131:             // Same deal as when fixed_strings is set above. If the pattern has
132:             // a line terminator anywhere, then we need to bail out and let
133:             // an error occur.
134:             if let Some(lineterm) = self.line_terminator {
135:                 if has_line_terminator(lineterm, p) {
136:                     return false;
137:                 }
138:             }
139:         }
140:         true

144: /// A "configured" HIR expression, which is aware of the configuration which
145: /// produced this HIR.
146: ///
147: /// Since the configuration is tracked, values with this type can be
148: /// transformed into other HIR expressions (or regular expressions) in a way
149: /// that preserves the configuration. For example, the `fast_line_regex`
150: /// method will apply literal extraction to the inner HIR and use that to build
151: /// a new regex that matches the extracted literals in a way that is
152: /// consistent with the configuration that produced this HIR. For example, the
153: /// size limits set on the configured HIR will be propagated out to any
154: /// subsequently constructed HIR or regular expression.
155: #[derive(Clone, Debug)]
156: pub(crate) struct ConfiguredHIR {

158:     hir: Hir,
159: }

161: impl ConfiguredHIR {
162:     /// Parse the given patterns into a single HIR expression that represents
163:     /// an alternation of the patterns given.
164:     fn new<P: AsRef<str>>(
165:         config: Config,
166:         patterns: &[P],
167:     ) -> Result<ConfiguredHIR, Error> {
168:         let hir = if config.is_fixed_strings(patterns) {
169:             let mut alts = vec![];
170:             for p in patterns.iter() {
171:                 alts.push(Hir::literal(p.as_ref().as_bytes()));
172:             }
173:             log::debug!(
174:                 "assembling HIR from {} fixed string literals",
175:                 alts.len()
176:             );
177:             let hir = Hir::alternation(alts);
178:             hir
179:         } else {
180:             let mut alts = vec![];
181:             for p in patterns.iter() {
182:                 alts.push(if config.fixed_strings {
183:                     format!("(?:{})", regex_syntax::escape(p.as_ref()))
184:                 } else {
185:                     format!("(?:{})", p.as_ref())
186:                 });
187:             }
188:             let pattern = alts.join("|");
189:             let ast = ast::parse::ParserBuilder::new()
190:                 .nest_limit(config.nest_limit)
191:                 .octal(config.octal)
192:                 .ignore_whitespace(config.ignore_whitespace)
193:                 .build()
194:                 .parse(&pattern)
195:                 .map_err(Error::generic)?;
196:             let analysis = AstAnalysis::from_ast(&ast);
197:             let mut hir = hir::translate::TranslatorBuilder::new()
198:                 .utf8(false)
199:                 .case_insensitive(config.is_case_insensitive(&analysis))
200:                 .multi_line(config.multi_line)
201:                 .dot_matches_new_line(config.dot_matches_new_line)
202:                 .crlf(config.crlf)
203:                 .swap_greed(config.swap_greed)
204:                 .unicode(config.unicode)
205:                 .build()
206:                 .translate(&pattern, &ast)
207:                 .map_err(Error::generic)?;
208:             // We don't need to do this for the fixed-strings case above
209:             // because is_fixed_strings will return false if any pattern
210:             // contains a line terminator. Therefore, we don't need to strip
211:             // it.
212:             //
213:             // We go to some pains to avoid doing this in the fixed-strings
214:             // case because this can result in building a new HIR when ripgrep
215:             // is given a huge set of literals to search for. And this can
216:             // actually take a little time. It's not huge, but it's noticeable.
217:             hir = match config.line_terminator {
218:                 None => hir,
219:                 Some(line_term) => strip_from_match(hir, line_term)?,
220:             };
221:             hir
222:         };

224:     }

227:     pub(crate) fn config(&self) -> &Config {

229:     }

22: pub(crate) struct WordMatcher {
23:     /// The regex which is roughly `(?:^|\W)(<original pattern>)(?:$|\W)`.
24:     regex: Regex,
25:     /// The HIR that produced the regex above. We don't keep the HIR for the
26:     /// `original` regex.
27:     ///
28:     /// We put this in an `Arc` because by the time it gets here, it won't
29:     /// change. And because cloning and dropping an `Hir` is somewhat expensive
30:     /// due to its deep recursive representation.
31:     chir: Arc<ConfiguredHIR>,
32:     /// The original regex supplied by the user, which we use in a fast path
33:     /// to try and detect matches before deferring to slower engines.
34:     original: Regex,
35:     /// A map from capture group name to capture group index.
36:     names: HashMap<String, usize>,
37:     /// A thread-safe pool of reusable buffers for finding the match offset of
38:     /// the inner group.
39:     caps: Arc<Pool<Captures, PoolFn>>,
40: }
41: 
42: impl Clone for WordMatcher {
43:     fn clone(&self) -> WordMatcher {
44:         // We implement Clone manually so that we get a fresh Pool such that it
45:         // can set its own thread owner. This permits each thread usings `caps`
46:         // to hit the fast path.
47:         //
48:         // Note that cloning a regex is "cheap" since it uses reference
49:         // counting internally.
50:         let re = self.regex.clone();
51:         WordMatcher {
52:             regex: self.regex.clone(),
53:             chir: Arc::clone(&self.chir),
54:             original: self.original.clone(),
55:             names: self.names.clone(),
56:             caps: Arc::new(Pool::new(Box::new(move || re.create_captures()))),
57:         }
58:     }
59: }
60: 
61: impl WordMatcher {
62:     /// Create a new matcher from the given pattern that only produces matches
63:     /// that are considered "words."
64:     ///
65:     /// The given options are used to construct the regular expression
66:     /// internally.
67:     pub(crate) fn new(chir: ConfiguredHIR) -> Result<WordMatcher, Error> {
68:         let original = chir.clone().into_anchored().to_regex()?;
69:         let chir = Arc::new(chir.into_word()?);
70:         let regex = chir.to_regex()?;
71:         let caps = Arc::new(Pool::new({
72:             let regex = regex.clone();
73:             Box::new(move || regex.create_captures()) as PoolFn
74:         }));
75: 
76:         let mut names = HashMap::new();
77:         let it = regex.group_info().pattern_names(PatternID::ZERO);
78:         for (i, optional_name) in it.enumerate() {
79:             if let Some(name) = optional_name {
80:                 names.insert(name.to_string(), i.checked_sub(1).unwrap());
81:             }
82:         }
83:         Ok(WordMatcher { regex, chir, original, names, caps })
84:     }
85: 
86:     /// Return the underlying regex used to match at word boundaries.
87:     ///
88:     /// The original regex is in the capture group at index 1.
89:     pub(crate) fn regex(&self) -> &Regex {
90:         &self.regex
91:     }
92: 
93:     /// Return the underlying HIR for the regex used to match at word
94:     /// boundaries.
95:     pub(crate) fn chir(&self) -> &ConfiguredHIR {
96:         &self.chir
97:     }
98: 
99:     /// Return the original user regex used to confirm inner word matches.
100:     pub(crate) fn original(&self) -> &Regex {
101:         &self.original
102:     }
103: }
104: 
105: impl Matcher for WordMatcher {
106:     type Captures = RegexCaptures;
107:     type Error = NoError;
108: 
109:     fn find_at(
110:         &self,
111:         haystack: &[u8],
112:         at: usize,
113:     ) -> Result<Option<Match>, NoError> {
114:         // To make this easy to get right, we extract captures here instead of
115:         // calling `find_at`. The actual match is at capture group `1` instead
116:         // of `0`. We *could* use `find_at` here and then trim the match after
117:         // the fact, but that's a bit harder to get right, and it's not clear
118:         // if it's worth it.
119:         //
120:         // OK, well, it turns out that it is worth it! But it is quite tricky.
121:         // See `fast_find` for details. Effectively, this lets us skip running
122:         // a slower regex engine to extract capture groups in the vast majority
123:         // of cases. However, the slower engine is I believe required for full
124:         // correctness.
125:         match self.chir.fast_find(self, haystack, at) {
126:             Ok(Some(m)) => return Ok(Some(m)),
127:             Ok(None) => return Ok(None),
128:             Err(()) => {}
129:         }
130: 
131:         let input = Input::new(haystack).span(at..haystack.len());
132:         let mut caps = self.caps.get();
133:         self.regex.search_captures(&input, &mut caps);
134:         Ok(caps.get_group(1).map(|sp| Match::new(sp.start, sp.end)))
135:     }
136: 
137:     fn new_captures(&self) -> Result<RegexCaptures, NoError> {
138:         Ok(RegexCaptures::with_offset(self.regex.create_captures(), 1))
139:     }
140: 
141:     fn capture_count(&self) -> usize {
142:         self.regex.captures_len().checked_sub(1).unwrap()
143:     }
144: 
145:     fn capture_index(&self, name: &str) -> Option<usize> {
146:         self.names.get(name).map(|i| *i)
147:     }
148: 
149:     fn captures_at(
150:         &self,
151:         haystack: &[u8],
152:         at: usize,
153:         caps: &mut RegexCaptures,
154:     ) -> Result<bool, NoError> {
155:         let input = Input::new(haystack).span(at..haystack.len());
156:         let caps = caps.captures_mut();
157:         self.regex.search_captures(&input, caps);
158:         Ok(caps.is_match())
159:     }
160: 
161:     // We specifically do not implement other methods like find_iter or
162:     // captures_iter. Namely, the iter methods are guaranteed to be correct
163:     // by virtue of implementing find_at and captures_at above.
164: }
